Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Review the epidemiology, etiology, pathophysiology, pathology, and risk factors associated
with femoral head osteonecrosis.
Explain the natural history, staging classification systems, and diagnostic evaluation of femoral
head osteonecrosis relevant to treatment decision making.
Discuss treatment options for different stages of osteonecrosis.
Overview
Osteonecrosis is bone necrosis or bone death, along with extensive cell death in the bone and
marrow space.
Adult femoral head osteonecrosis is the most prevalent and problematic type clinically and is
the focus of this lesson.




This lesson also reviews a pediatric form of femoral head osteonecrosis called Legg-Calvé-
Perthes (LCPD) disease.
In this lesson, the terms osteonecrosis and femoral head osteonecrosis will be used
interchangeably.

Overview
The term osteonecrosis (bone death) is preferred over the terms avascular necrosis,
ischemic necrosis, or aseptic necrosis because it does not specify an etiology. Although
osteonecrosis primarily is induced by a loss of blood supply (ie, avascular or ischemic
necrosis), other etiologic factors, such as irradiation and excessive heat, also can induce
osteonecrosis. Osteonecrosis can affect various regions of the pediatric and adult
skeleton. Some etiologic factors, such as corticosteroids and sickle cell disease, can
result in multi-site, polyostotic osteonecrosis. Adult femoral head osteonecrosis is the
most prevalent and problematic type of osteonecrosis clinically. A pediatric form of
idiopathic femoral head osteonecrosis, called LCPD, is the most common form of
childhood femoral head osteonecrosis. LCPD produces a permanent residual femoral
head deformity and hip osteoarthritis in adulthood.
Adult Osteonecrosis
Epidemiology
In the United States, 10,000 to 20,000 new cases are diagnosed each year1,2 (Video 1).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:29 PM
AAOS | Osteonecrosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002104
2/32

Video 1 Jones LC: Moving forward in osteonecrosis: What research is telling us, from Goodman
SB, mod: New paradigms in the etiology, pathogenesis, and treatment of osteonecrosis.
Presented at the Annual Meeting of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, New
Orleans, LA, March 6-10, 2018.

Epidemiology
Femoral head osteonecrosis primarily affects patients aged 30 to 50 years.
Approximately 80% of cases are associated with corticosteroid therapy or alcohol abuse,
with corticosteroids being associated with approximately 40% of patients. Femoral head
osteonecrosis accounts for approximately 10% of total hip arthroplasty (THA) procedures
in the United States each year.
Etiology
Osteonecrosis can be divided into traumatic and nontraumatic etiologies.
Nontraumatic etiologies include corticosteroid therapy, sickle cell disease, fat emboli,
coagulation disorders, nitrogen bubbles (bends), and hypercoagulable states. head from
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:29 PM
AAOS | Osteonecrosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002104
3/32

trauma, such as hip dislocation or femoral neck fracture.

Etiology
Traumatic etiologies produce mechanical disruption of the blood vessels supplying the
femoral head from trauma, such as hip dislocation or femoral neck fracture.
Nontraumatic etiologies may affect arterial, venous, and/or cellular components of the
femoral head. Each nontraumatic etiology may work via one specific mechanism or a
combination of mechanisms to produce osteonecrosis; this is the case with
corticosteroid therapy. The following nontraumatic etiologies produce arterial vessel
occlusion, microvascular thrombus, or intravascular coagulation: nitrogen bubbles
(bends), sickle cell disease, fat emboli, coagulation disorders, and hypercoagulable
states. Corticosteroid therapy, vasculitis, and radiation injury may cause vascular
endothelial cell damage. In addition, corticosteroid therapy has been shown to cause
osteocyte apoptosis. Bone marrow disorder from Gaucher disease and corticosteroid
therapy may increase intraosseous pressure or extravascular compression from altered
lipid metabolism and lipid accumulation in the marrow and produce venous outflow
obstruction because of increased intracapsular or intraosseous pressure.
Blood Supply to the Femoral Head
The deep branch of the medial femoral circumflex artery provides most of the blood supply to
the adult femoral head.
The deep branch terminates at the superior or lateral retinacular arteries. 

Blood Supply to the Femoral Head
In most patients, the deep femoral artery gives rise to the medial and lateral femoral
circumflex arteries, which provide blood supply to the femoral head. The deep branch of
the medial femoral circumflex artery provides most of the blood supply to the adult
femoral head. The deep branch further divides and terminates as the posterior superior
nutrient arteries.3 These arteries also are referred to as the superior or lateralSEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:29 PM
AAOS | Osteonecrosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002104
4/32

retinacular arteries because they course along the femoral neck surface within the
retinaculum. They enter the femoral head through the vascular foramina close to the
head-neck junction in the posterior-superior and anterior-superior quadrants of the
femoral head.4 Within the femoral head, some surgeons refer to these vessels as the
lateral epiphyseal artery. The lateral femoral circumflex artery gives rise to the anterior
nutrient arteries and, along with the artery of ligamentum teres from the obturator
artery, they represent a minor component of the blood supply to the femoral head. The
anterolateral quadrant of the femoral head is most predisposed to osteonecrosis as a
watershed region.
Pathophysiology of Corticosteroid-Induced Osteonecrosis
Corticosteroids work via multiple pathogenic mechanisms that involve cell death, vascular
function, immune function, lipid metabolism, adipogenesis, and coagulation.
Individual host factors, such as genetic predisposition, may play a role in the pathogenesis.

Pathophysiology of Corticosteroid-Induced Osteonecrosis
Corticosteroids produce cellular, hematologic, and immunologic effects via their ability
to influence gene transcription involving apoptosis,5 immune function, lipid metabolism,
adipogenesis, and coagulation. Corticosteroids are known to alter the function and
survival of bone osteocytes, osteoblasts, and osteoclasts and other cells, including
immune cells, vascular endothelial cells, and adipocytes.6,7,8 A common pathway in
corticosteroid-induced osteonecrosis is cell death and compromised blood flow to the
bone. With regard to its effect on the vascular system, corticosteroids can cause direct
endothelial cell injury, resulting in a decrease in the number of functional microvessels.
Damage to the endothelial cells also can result in increased vascular resistance;
increased thrombin, platelet aggregation, and thrombosis; and decreased blood flow by
affecting the production of vasoactive factors, such as nitric oxide, endothelin,
bradykinin, and prostacyclin.8 Corticosteroid therapy also can affect the repair process
by decreasing the synthesis of vascular endothelial growth factor and the subsequent
inhibition of new capillary growth.7 At high doses, corticosteroids act to inhibit the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:29 PM
AAOS | Osteonecrosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002104
5/32

fibrinolytic pathway via an increase in the activity of plasma plasminogen activator
inhibitor and a reduction in tissue plasminogen activator activity.8 This process results in
decreased conversion of plasminogen to plasmin, decreased fibrinolysis, and increased
thrombosis. The subsequent hypofibrinogenolysis is associated with a reduction of
femoral head blood flow, a hypercoagulable state, and osteonecrosis. In addition,
corticosteroids induce adipogenesis of mesenchymal progenitor cells.9 Accumulation of
fatty tissue in the femoral head, fat emboli, and the procoagulant effect of adipocyte
breakdown particles have been implicated in the etiology of osteonecrosis.8 Note that
osteonecrosis does not develop in most patients treated with corticosteroids for various
medical conditions. Studies suggest that, along with the dose and duration of
corticosteroid therapy, individual host factors, such as genetic predisposition, may play a
considerable role in the pathogenesis.10 Multiple genetic polymorphisms have been
reported to be associated with an increased or reduced risk of osteonecrosis. Because
many of the studies are based on a relatively small sample size and have no conclusive
confirmatory results, the true importance of genetic involvement remains unclear.
Pathology
Pathologic features of osteonecrosis depend on the stage of osteonecrosis (Tables 1 and 2).
Three identifiable histologic zones: necrotic, reparative or reactive, and viable.

Pathology
Macroscopic assessment of femoral head specimens typically reveals a wedge-shaped
necrotic area in the subchondral region that appears yellow in color compared with the
brown/reddish color of the viable bone. Microscopic assessment of the necrotic area and
its bordering area typically reveals three identifiable zones: necrotic, reparative or
reactive, and viable. In the necrotic zone, the marrow space is acellular, with remnant
extracellular matrix and necrotic cell debris. The trabeculae in the necrotic region lack
lining by osteoblasts or osteoclasts. The lacunae of the necrotic bone are empty or
contain dead osteocyte with pyknotic nuclei. In the reparative or reactive zone,
fibrovascular granulation tissue is observed in the marrow space with appositional bone
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:29 PM
AAOS | Osteonecrosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002104
6/32

formation (active osteoblasts) on the surface of the necrotic trabeculae, producing
thickening of the trabeculae. The term creeping substitution refers to the slow reparative
process of replacing necrotic bone with new bone. In general, the reparative process is
limited, and progressive advance of the repair process into the necrotic zone does not
occur. In the early stage of osteonecrosis, infiltration of the necrotic marrow space by
endothelial cells, mesenchymal cells, and immune cells, such as macrophages, is
observed. In the viable zone, living cells are observed, with the possible alteration of the
marrow content, such as decreased hematopoietic cells and increased adipocytes and
fat because of the underlying etiology of osteonecrosis. Along with femoral head
pathology, hip joint synovitis and effusion are common features of osteonecrosis. In the
late stage (stage 3) of osteonecrosis, structural failure, such as subchondral fracture and
segmental collapse of the femoral head, are observed. In stage 4, degenerative changes
in the articular cartilage and joint are observed, with bone-on-bone erosion of cartilage,
osteophyte formation, and acetabular degenerative changes.
Pathogenesis of Subchondral Fracture and Collapse
Microfracture accumulation, osteoclastic resorption, and the development of stress riser at the
junction of the necrotic and the reparative zone have been proposed as potential mechanisms
for the development of subchondral fracture and collapse.

Pathogenesis of Subchondral Fracture and Collapse
A large animal study showed an accumulation of microfracture or microcracks in the
subchondral bone because of alternation of the mechanical and material properties of
the necrotic bone.11 The subchondral bone had considerably increased mineral
(calcium), which made it more brittle and prone to microfracture. Osteoclastic resorption
of the necrotic bone in the subchondral region at the junction of the necrotic zone and
the reparative zone also can weaken the bone in combination with the stress riser at the
junction of the necrotic bone and thickened trabecular bone in the reparative zone.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:29 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002104
7/32

Risk Factors and Associated Conditions
Several risk factors and conditions are associated with osteonecrosis.

Risk Factors and Associated Conditions
Risk factors include genetic predisposition, corticosteroid use, alcohol abuse, radiation
therapy, chemotherapy, and organ transplantation. Associated conditions include sickle
cell disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, hypercoagulable conditions,
thromboembolic disorders, hyperlipidemia syndromes, HIV, Gaucher disease, and
Caisson disease.
Natural History
The size and location of the necrotic lesion affect the rate of collapse of the femoral head.
The lesion size and location also are associated with symptom development.

Natural History
A systematic review of published articles on asymptomatic hips found that 84% of large
lesions (defined as >50% of the femoral head size) progressed or collapsed over a mean
weighted follow-up period of 88 months compared with only 7% of small lesions (defined
as <25% of the femoral head size).12 Necrotic lesions located in the lateral third of the
femoral head were more likely to progress or collapse than those in the medial third of
the femoral head (59% versus 9%). Overall, approximately 60% of asymptomatic and
80% of symptomatic hips progressed to segmental femoral head collapse (stage 3) and
degenerative osteoarthritis (stage 4). Spontaneous resolution has been shown to occur
but rarely and only with very small lesions.13
Staging Classification Systems
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:29 PM
AAOS | Osteonecrosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002104
8/32

Three commonly used staging systems are the Ficat classification system (oldest), the
Steinberg classification system (also known as the University of Pennsylvania classification
system), and the Association Research Circulation Osseous classification system.14
A staging classification system should provide prognostic information, guide treatment decision
making, and be associated with high interobserver and intraobserver reliability. Many staging
systems have been proposed; however, no consensus exists on the best classification system
because of their modest interobserver reliability and limitations. Newer classification systems
incorporate abnormal changes in the femoral head detected on radiographs, bone scans, CT
scans, and/or MRIs, along with the percentage of head involvement and/or the amount of head
depression. Information on the 2019 Revised Association Research Circulation Osseous
Classification of Adult Osteonecrosis and the Steinberg Classification of Adult Osteonecrosis and
related progression of femoral head osteonecrosis is provided in Tables 1 and 2.15

Patient Evaluation
Patient History
Diagnosis of osteonecrosis requires a patient history, physical examination, and diagnostic
imaging studies.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:29 PM
AAOS | Osteonecrosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002104
10/32

The nature of pain may change from a dull, aching pain to a severe arthritic pain with a
collapse of the femoral head and the development of osteoarthritis.

Patient History
Most patients present with pain; however, the duration of pain does not generally reflect
the duration of the disease process. Patients rarely present at the time of the onset of
osteonecrosis or shortly after, indicating that bone necrosis itself is not a pain-
generating event in most patients and that pain is not a sensitive indicator of the onset
of osteonecrosis. In some patients, asymptomatic osteonecrosis is found incidentally or
at the time of diagnostic imaging of the contralateral symptomatic hip. Wide variability in
the duration of the asymptomatic period has been reported in patients who were
exposed to a known risk factor for osteonecrosis, such as solid organ transplantation
and corticosteroid therapy. Potential causes of pain include increased marrow pressure
and edema, the development of hip synovitis and effusion related to osteonecrosis,
subchondral fracture and collapse, and degenerative joint disease. Pain generally
precedes femoral head collapse. With disease progression, the nature of pain may
change from a dull, aching pain in the joint to a severe arthritic pain with collapse of the
joint and the development of osteoarthritis. In later stages of the disease, pain may
severely affect sleep and daily activities. Physical examination should include assessment
of gait; hip range of motion, especially abduction and rotation; signs of hip impingement;
and hip muscle weakness.
Diagnostic Imaging Studies
Plain radiography is the first-line diagnostic imaging modality and is useful for monitoring the
progression of the disease.
MRI is the preferred multiplanar imaging modality for the detection of the precollapse stage of
osteonecrosis because of its high sensitivity in assessment of the location and size of the
lesion.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:29 PM
AAOS | Osteonecrosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002104
11/32


Diagnostic Imaging Studies
Various imaging modalities are used to assess femoral head osteonecrosis. Plain
radiography is the initial imaging modality used for diagnosis and management. AP
pelvis and frog-leg lateral views are recommended. Characteristic radiographic findings
in the femoral head, such as sclerosis, cyst formation, subchondral fracture or collapse,
and arthritic changes, are used to stage disease progression and are integral aspects of
various staging classification systems (Tables 1 and 2). In the early stage of
osteonecrosis, especially in the pre-radiographic stage, the sensitivity of radiography is
low, and the ability to quantify the amount of femoral head involvement via radiography
is limited. In general, plain radiographs should be supplemented by MRIs for accurate
staging and assessment of the location and size of the lesion and for patients with
normal radiographs in whom osteonecrosis is suspected. Other imaging modalities, such
as MRI, CT, bone scintigraphy, or positron emission tomography and CT, may be
performed for various indications. In the United States, MRI has become the preferred
multiplanar imaging modality for the detection of osteonecrosis, assessment of the
extent of involvement, and staging because of its high sensitivity and specificity and the
availability of various sequences to assess the marrow changes, vascularity, soft tissues,
articular cartilage, and synovitis in the joint. The basic MRI sequences include T1-
weighted and T2-weighted images. Newer sequences and techniques, such as short tau
inversion recovery and gadolinium-enhanced MRI (perfusion MRI), also are being
performed at some centers to delineate the pathologic and repair processes. On T2-
weighted images, the double-line sign, consisting of an inner rim with a high signal
intensity and an outer rim with a low-signal intensity is characteristic of osteonecrosis.
CT is useful for delineating subchondral fracture because it has been shown to be more
sensitive than MRI in the detection of subchondral fractures. Bone scintigraphy
previously was performed in patients with normal radiographs in whom a high suspicion
for osteonecrosis existed (stage 1). Bone scintigraphy has been superseded by MRI,
which is associated with greater sensitivity and specificity and provides better imaging of
other features of osteonecrosis. 
Differential Diagnosis
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:29 PM
AAOS | Osteonecrosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002104
12/32

Bone marrow edema syndrome and transient osteoporosis of the hip
Subchondral insufficiency fracture

Differential Diagnosis
Bone marrow edema syndrome is a rare condition that is more common in males. In
females, it typically occurs in the third trimester of pregnancy. Its natural history is
spontaneous resolution. Subchondral insufficiency fractures are observed in elderly
patients with osteoporosis and in renal transplant recipients.
Management
Treatment Decision Making
Treatment decisions should consider the stage of disease (precollapse versus postcollapse),
the size of lesion, the extent of collapse, the age of the patient, and patient comorbidities.
(Video 2)
Nonsurgical treatment is indicated only in patients with small lesions.
Surgical management is based on the stage of disease.
Currently, no established or widely accepted medical therapy is available for the management
of osteonecrosis.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:29 PM
AAOS | Osteonecrosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002104
13/32

Video 2 Goodman SB: Osteonecrosis, from Goodman SB, mod: New paradigms in the etiology,
pathogenesis and treatment of osteonecrosis. Presented at the Annual Meeting of the American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, Las Vegas, NV, March 12-16, 2019.

Treatment Decision Making
The natural history of femoral head osteonecrosis is to collapse and progress to
osteoarthritis unless the lesion is small, medially located, or away from the subchondral
region. Therefore, nonsurgical treatment is indicated only in patients with small lesions.
For small lesions, observation is appropriate because spontaneous resolution has been
shown to occur and a low risk for progression to collapse exists.13 Treatment options for
the precollapse stage are core decompression, core decompression with adjuvant
concentrated bone marrow cellular grafting via injection, multiple small diameter drilling,
nonvascularized or vascularized bone grafting, and osteotomy. Treatment options for
mild collapse of less than 2 mm include nonvascularized or vascularized bone grafting,
osteotomy, and total hip replacement. The outcomes of hip preservation procedures
instituted at this stage are not as good as those instituted at the precollapse stage. THA
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:29 PM
AAOS | Osteonecrosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002104
14/32

is the preferred treatment option for patients with late collapse stage and osteoarthritic
changes (stage 4). 
Core Decompression and Variations

Core Decompression and Variations
Core decompression for the management of adult femoral head osteonecrosis was
reported in the early 1970s by Arlet et al16 to be a procedure to relieve the elevated
intraosseous pressure of the femoral head and stimulate necrotic bone healing. The
conventional technique involves removal of an 8- to 10-mm diameter longitudinal core
with the use of a trephine or a reamer along the femoral neck to the central region of
femoral head necrosis. Additional removal of the necrotic bone via curettage and
burring, followed by the packing of morselized cancellous autograft, allograft, or
synthetic bone substitute have been advocated by some surgeons. Some surgeons also
advocate arthroscopic-assisted core decompression (Video 3). One of the concerns with
this technique is the acute loss of structural integrity of the femoral head because of the
large amount of native bone that must be removed. As an alternative to conventional
core decompression, some surgeons advocate the use of multiple, small, 3-mm diameter
drillings.17 This procedure is associated with the theoretic advantage of reducing the
mechanical instability created by removing a large core of bone. Another advantage is
the increased distribution of bone channels for vascular invasion and the migration of
repair cells from viable bone in the metaphysis. The multiple small drillings procedure
has been shown to result in success rates for stage I and stage II osteonecrosis similar to
those reported via conventional core decompression techniques.18 The risks of
subtrochanteric fracture and inadvertent penetration or blowout of the femoral head
associated with a large core technique may be decreased with multiple small drillings.
Another variation of the conventional core decompression technique is to use a 4-mm
trocar to create a tunnel to the center of the necrosis, followed by injection of
autologous bone marrow concentrate.19 A recent systematic review and meta-analysis
of 32 published articles on the outcomes of core decompression with or without
autologous bone or bone marrow cell transplantation reported an overall success rate of

Adjunctive Bone Marrow Stromal Cell Therapy

Adjunctive Bone Marrow Stromal Cell Therapy
Bone marrow is a source of mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs). In the adult population, the
number of MSCs in the bone marrow is low, ranging from 1 per 10,000 to 1 per
1,000,000 mononuclear cells.21Because increasing the number of MSCs for
transplantation has been shown to result in better bone regeneration outcomes, bone
marrow aspirate is concentrated to create a bone marrow aspirate concentrate
containing an increased concentration of MSCs. The bone marrow aspiration technique
used may greatly affect the number of MSCs collected from bone marrow. Higher
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:29 PM
AAOS | Osteonecrosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002104
16/32

numbers of MSCs are obtained by aspirating a smaller, 2-mL volume of bone marrow
aspirate at a given needle site to minimize peripheral blood dilution.22 A recent
systematic review and meta-analysis of 16 published articles on patients with stage I or
stage II (precollapse stage) osteonecrosis showed that core decompression in addition to
bone marrow stromal cell therapy resulted in a substantially lower hip pain score, a
higher Harris hip score, and a lower number of patients progressing to THA compared
with core decompression alone.23 Major limitations of current adjuvant MSC therapies
for osteonecrosis are nonstandardized techniques for bone marrow aspiration and
processing and lack of quality control for the number of MSCs transplanted (Video 4).
Video 4 Hernigou P: Osteonecrosis repair with stem cells: 30 years of experience with
bone marrow concentration, from Goodman SB, mod: New paradigms in the etiology,
pathogenesis and treatment of osteonecrosis. Presented at the Annual Meeting of the
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, Las Vegas, NV, March 12-16, 2019.
Nonvascularized Bone Grafting

Nonvascularized Bone Grafting
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:29 PM
AAOS | Osteonecrosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002104
17/32

bone grafting is a treatment option for precollapse and postcollapse osteonecrosis that
is a distinct procedure from core decompression with adjuvant bone grafting. Various
bone grafts and techniques have been described, including nonvascularized fibular graft,
cortical strut grafts, and the packing of morselized cancellous bone grafts. More
advanced bone grafting techniques include the lightbulb and trapdoor procedures.
Although short-term results appear to be promising, the number of studies reporting the
results of these techniques and the durations of follow-up are limited.
Vascularized Bone Grafting

Vascularized Bone Grafting
Vascularized bone grafting is a conceptually appealing option because it allows for the
removal of the necrotic bone and replacement with vascularized bone, potentially
speeding up the healing process. Various anatomic sources and techniques have been
described, including free vascularized fibular graft and vascularized bone pedicle derived
from the ileum or the greater trochanter. Successful short-term and intermediate-term
outcomes range from 70% to 90%; however, most studies include a small number of
patients. Treatment considerations include technical difficulties associated with vascular
anastomosis, ideal placement of the graft in the femoral head, preparation and bone
grafting of the adjacent necrotic region, long surgical duration, and potential harvest site
morbidity.
Proximal Femoral Osteotomy

Proximal Femoral Osteotomy
Proximal femoral osteotomy via intertrochanteric or rotational osteotomy techniques
have been advocated by some surgeons to manage osteonecrosis, including
postcollapse osteonecrosis (stage 3). The treatment concept is to rotate the necrotic or
collapsed region of the femoral head away from the high-loading region of the hip joint.
Good outcomes have been reported; however, technical challenges and non- SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:29 PM
AAOS | Osteonecrosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002104
18/32

reproducibility of the results limit wide acceptance and use. An important consideration
is the potential consequence of proximal femoral osteotomy on future THA.
Total Hip Arthroplasty

Total Hip Arthroplasty
THA is the preferred treatment option for symptomatic patients in the postcollapse
stage who have osteoarthritic changes (stage 4) or symptomatic, older patients in a
precollapse stage who have a large necrotic lesion and/or comorbidities. Because
necrotic lesions may extend beyond the femoral head in patients with certain diagnoses,
such as corticosteroid osteonecrosis and sickle cell disease, preoperative MRI is useful to
define the extent of femoral neck/metaphyseal involvement. Intermediate-term
outcomes after THA in patients with osteonecrosis are comparable with those after THA
in patients with other diagnoses.
Medical Therapy

Medical Therapy
Several drug therapies have been described, including diphosphonates, statins,
anticoagulants, and vasodilators. Systemic diphosphonate therapy is one of the most
studied pharmacologic therapies. The positive effects of diphosphonate therapy in
preventing or minimizing femoral head deformity and preserving bone volume have
been shown in various animal models of osteonecrosis; however, a recent meta-analysis
of seven published clinical trials on systemic diphosphonate therapy found no
considerable difference in pain control, Harris hip score, radiographic progression, or
the rate of THA between the diphosphonate therapy group and the control group.24
Because of a lack of blood flow to the necrotic region of the femoral head, experimental
studies have shown that the systemic administration of diphosphonates is ineffective for
the drug bioavailability in the necrotic region, whereas local intraosseous delivery was
effective.25,26 This finding may partially explain the reason systemic diphosphonate

Legg-Calvé-Perthes Disease
Epidemiology and Etiology
LCPD affects children aged 1.5 to 15 years27 (Resource 1).
The etiology is unknown.

Epidemiology and Etiology
LCPD most commonly affects children aged 4 to 8 years. It is four to five times more
common in boys than girls, with an occurrence rate of 1 in 740 boys and 1 in 3,500 girls.
The incidence varies depending on the region and ranges from 0 to 15 per 100,000
children. Bilateral disease will develop in 10% to 15% of patients, either concurrently (in
both hips at the same time) or sequentially (one hip after the other). It is unlikely to be
an inherited disorder because less than 5% of patients have a family history of LCPD. A
twin registry study by Metcalfe et al28 showed no concordance between one identical
twin with LCPD and the other identical twin. Currently, a multifactorial etiology, with
genetic predisposition and environmental influence, is suspected.
Pathophysiology, Pathology, and Pathogenesis of Femoral Head
Deformity
Pathology
A disruption of blood supply to the femoral head produces osteonecrosis and growth arrest of
the femoral epiphysis.
Chronic hip synovitis is a consistent feature of LCPD and results in hip pain, hip joint irritability,
and decreased motion.29

Mechanical weakening and development of the femoral head deformity occurs in the
avascular and vascular phases of the disease (Figure 1).


Pathology
A disruption of blood flow to the juvenile femoral head produces osteonecrosis of the
bony epiphysis and chondronecrosis of the deep layer of the immature articular
cartilage, which consists of the epiphyseal cartilage (growth cartilage).30 This process
explains the reason the affected femoral epiphysis is smaller in size than the unaffected
side. The proximal femoral physis and the metaphysis also may be affected in some
patients, manifesting as proximal femoral growth disturbance and producing coxa breva
and metaphyseal radiolucency or a cyst, respectively. Substantial joint synovitis may be
present in the early stage of the disease, along with elevation of proinflammatory
cytokine interleukin-6 and persistence of hip synovitis for more than 1 year.29 Over time,
invasion by vascular granulation tissue from the periphery of the femoral head occurs,

necrotic bone in the anterocentral region of the femoral epiphysis is the last to resorb
and reossify.
Pathogenesis of Femoral Head Deformity

Pathogenesis of Femoral Head Deformity
Mechanical weakening and development of the femoral head deformity occurs in the
avascular and vascular phases of the disease.31 In the avascular phase, chondronecrosis
of the deep layer of the immature articular cartilage, alteration of the material properties
of the calcified cartilage and trabecular bone in the necrotic femoral head, and
accumulation of microcracks in the necrotic bone from repetitive loading are thought to
mechanically weaken the femoral epiphysis and contribute to subchondral fracture and
early compression deformity of the necrotic epiphysis in the avascular stage.32,33 A
substantial increase in the mineral content of the necrotic bone and the brittleness of
the bone has been reported, along with increased microcracks in a piglet model of
LCPD.11,34
In the vascular phase, gradual revascularization of the necrotic femoral head and
subsequent resorption of the necrotic bone along with delayed new bone formation
further weaken the mechanical properties of the necrotic head. The imbalance between
bone resorption and new bone formation produces a net bone loss, observed
radiographically as a radiolucent area within the necrotic bone in the fragmentation
stage, during which most of the femoral head deformity occurs. Because the hip joint is
a major load-bearing joint, development of the femoral head deformity in the context of
the amount of loading of the joint must be considered. Increased loading of the joint has
been postulated to result in a greater deformity. In a piglet model of LCPD, decreasing
the loading of the affected hip considerably reduced the femoral head deformity.35

The age at onset of the disease, the degree of femoral head deformity, the extent of femoral
head involvement, and lateral pillar height are important prognostic factors.31

Natural History
Patients who were younger than 6 years at the onset of LCPD have a better prognosis. A
study by McAndrew and Weinstein36 with a mean follow-up of 47 years found that 40%
of patients maintained a good level of function (Iowa Hip Score >80 points), whereas 40%
of patients had already undergone arthroplasty, 10% had disabling osteoarthritis, and
the remaining 10% had an Iowa Hip Score of less than 80 points. A study by Mose37
found that 12%, 22%, and 100% of femoral heads with irregular shapes at healing had
radiographic evidence of osteoarthritis at a mean follow-up of 17, 27, and 57 years,
respectively. A study by Stulberg et al38 reported a correlation between the shape or
deformity of the femoral head at skeletal maturity and the long-term risk for
osteoarthritis. The authors reported a substantial decline in radiographic outcomes from
spherical femoral heads (class I or class II hips), which are considered good results, to
nonspherical femoral heads (class III to class V hips), which are considered fair to poor
results.
Common Classification Systems
The Waldenström staging system consists of four temporal radiographic stages of LCPD: the
initial or the osteonecrosis stage, the stage of fragmentation, the stage of reossification, and
the healed stage.
The lateral pillar classification system is based on the height of the lateral 15% to 30% of the
epiphysis, termed the lateral pillar.
The Stulberg Radiographic Outcome Classification System is a five-class classification system
based on the severity of the femoral head deformity and loss of hip joint congruence assessed
via radiographs obtained at skeletal maturity.38

Radiographic features of the initial or avascular stage (stage 1) of LCPD include a smaller
femoral epiphysis, increased radiodensity, and a widened space between the epiphysis
and the medial acetabulum compared with the unaffected side. A crescent sign is
observed in 30% of patients. Radiographic features of the fragmentation stage (stage 2)
of LCPD include mild to severe flattening of the femoral epiphysis, a fragmented
appearance of the epiphysis with radiolucent areas from bone resorption, lateral
extrusion or subluxation of the epiphysis, and increased medial joint space.
Radiographic features of the reossification stage (stage 3) of LCPD include the
appearance of new small ossifications in the periphery of the femoral epiphysis, with a
gradual increase of ossified areas in the femoral head and the disappearance of the
fragmented epiphysis. Radiographic features of the healed stage (stage 4) of LCPD
include complete reossification of the femoral head with homogeneous radiodensity. In
skeletally immature patients, the shape of the femoral head may continue to evolve.31 A
modified Waldenström staging system further divides each stage into early (A) and late
(B) stages. The modified staging system is associated with very good interobserver and
intraobserver reliability and is useful in treatment decision making.39 The lateral pillar
classification originally was described by Herring et al40,41 as a three-category system
comprised of groups A, B, and C, with a later addition of group B/C. It is based on the
height of the lateral 15% to 30% of the epiphysis, termed the lateral pillar. In group A, no
loss of lateral pillar height occurs. In group B, less than 50% of lateral pillar height is lost.
In group B/C, 50% of lateral pillar height is lost. In group C, more than 50% of lateral
pillar height is lost. The classification system should be applied to AP radiographs
obtained at the mid to late fragmentation stage, at which the extent of femoral head
deformity has stabilized. Application of the classification at earlier stages is less reliable.
A substantial correlation exists between the lateral pillar classification system and
subsequent Stulberg radiographic outcome. Group A hips had the best outcomes; group
B hips had an intermediate outcomes; and group C hips had the poorest outcomes. The
Stulberg Radiographic Outcome Classification System is based on the severity of the
femoral head deformity and loss of hip joint congruence assessed via radiographs
obtained at skeletal maturity.38 Class I represents a normal hip joint. Class II represents
a spherical femoral head with enlargement, a short neck, or a steep acetabulum. Class III
represents a nonspherical head (ovoid, mushroom, or umbrella shaped). Class IV
represents a flat head, and Class V represents a flat head with an incongruent hip joint.
This classification system correlates with the development of radiographic signs of

Diagnostic Imaging Studies
Radiography is the first-line diagnostic imaging modality. AP pelvis and frog-leg lateral views
are recommended.
Perfusion MRI can be used to quantify the amount of femoral head involvement based on
hypoperfusion and to predict outcomes.42,43

Diagnostic Imaging Studies
Plain radiography is useful for diagnosis and monitoring of the progression of the
disease. AP pelvis and frog-leg lateral views are recommended. Early femoral head
deformity and the crescent sign (subchondral fracture) are best observed on frog-leg
lateral radiographs. MRI, especially gadolinium-enhanced MRI (perfusion MRI), is helpful
in the early stage of the disease during which diagnosis is questionable. Perfusion MRI
also can be performed in the early stage to quantify the amount of femoral head
involvement based on hypoperfusion and to predict outcomes.42,43 MRI also is useful in
assessing symptomatic patients in the healed stage of LCPD because of
femoroacetabular impingement and labral pathology or an osteochondritis dissecans–
type lesion in the central region of the femoral head.
Differential Diagnosis
LCPD is a diagnosis of exclusion.

Differential Diagnosis
Known causes of juvenile osteonecrosis along with other conditions that mimic LCPD
must be ruled out via a careful patient history, physical examination, and diagnostic

arthritis or subacute osteomyelitis; chondrolysis; juvenile rheumatoid arthritis; traumatic
osteonecrosis secondary to hip fracture or dislocation; corticosteroid-associated
osteonecrosis because of leukemia treatment and inflammatory conditions;
osteonecrosis associated with sickle cell disease; iatrogenic osteonecrosis from prior hip
surgery for developmental dysplasia of the hip and slipped capital femoral epiphysis;
tumor or tumor-like conditions affecting the proximal femoral epiphysis or acetabulum
(eg, osteoid osteoma, chondroblastoma, bone cyst); skeletal dysplasias, such as multiple
epiphyseal dysplasia, trichorhinophalangeal syndrome, and spondyloepiphyseal
dysplasia; Gaucher disease; and hypothyroidism.
Management
In general, patients who are younger than 6 years at onset tend to have better outcomes than
patients who are 8 years or older at onset.
Patients who are older than 10 years at onset have the poorest prognosis.

Management
Treatment plan depends on the age at onset of LCPD, the stage of the disease, hip range
of motion, and social factors. Initial treatment of patients may include rest; activity
restrictions; weight-bearing relief via crutches, a walker, or a wheelchair; and gentle
range of motion exercises. Treatment goals are to restore and maintain good hip range
of motion, especially hip abduction, and to prevent or minimize the deformity of the
femoral head. NSAIDs should be used judiciously because chronic use may inhibit new
bone formation. In patients with restricted hip abduction, a wide abduction Petrie cast is
used to rest the inflamed hip joint, to contain the femoral head in the acetabulum, and
to regain hip abduction. Some surgeons recommend the use of a part-time wide
abduction A-frame brace for a prolonged duration after the removal of the Petrie cast.42
Surgical treatment27 for patients in the active stage of LCPD (stages 1 to 3) include
femoral osteotomies (proximal femoral varus or valgus osteotomy), pelvic osteotomies
(Salter or triple osteotomy), and shelf acetabuloplasty. Indications for specific surgical
procedures depend on patient age, disease stage, hip motion, the amount of femoral
